title: Getting paid to wait - selling puts where you would buy, selling calls on what you hold (premiums modelled, not measured)
rule_plain: A put you SELL is a promise to buy SPY at a set price [the strike] on a set date; you are paid a fee [the premium] up front for making it, and the full purchase price waits in Treasury bills meanwhile [cash-secured].
A call you SELL on shares you own is a promise to sell them at a set price on a set date; you are paid a premium, and give up any rise beyond that price [covered call].
Every 21 sessions (about a month) the rule sells a fresh 21-session option at the close and the old one settles on that same close. Nothing is predicted: the calendar alone decides the day.
Put at the money: always in cash, promising to buy at today's close. If SPY ends lower, the shortfall is paid from the cash; SPY is never owned (the Cboe PutWrite index works this way).
Put 2% below: the same with the promise set 2% under today's close - a smaller premium, and the first 2% of a fall costs nothing.
Covered call 2% above: hold SPY all the time and promise to sell 2% over today's close; a month's rise beyond 2% is paid away in cash and the shares are kept.
In the covered-call run each premium is used at once to buy more SPY, and a payment owed at settlement is met by selling a few shares.

The wheel: sell puts 2% below while in cash; if SPY ends under the strike you buy there. While holding, sell calls 2% above; if SPY ends over the strike the shares go at that price and you are back in cash selling puts.

We hold no option prices, so every premium is MODELLED, not measured: the standard option formula [Black-Scholes] fed with the market's own fear gauge [the VIX] at that close, then cut by 5% for the dealing spread and commission.
The account is revalued with the same model at every close, so the falls shown are daily, not just month-end.

variants.label: Always in cash, selling a monthly promise to buy SPY at today's price (cash-secured put - premiums modelled, not measured)
variants.note: Every 21 sessions: sell puts [a promise to buy] struck at that close on the whole account, cash in bills, settled in cash 21 sessions later; never owns SPY. Premiums are modelled from the VIX, not measured. This is where the model is most generous to the seller - see the caveats and the measured Cboe index.

variants.label: Always in cash, selling a monthly promise to buy SPY 2% below today's price (cash-secured put - premiums modelled, not measured)
variants.note: Same, with the strike [the promised buying price] set 2% under that close. Premiums are modelled from the VIX, not measured.

variants.label: Always holding SPY, selling a monthly promise to sell it 2% above today's price (covered call - premiums modelled, not measured)
variants.note: Holds SPY throughout. Every 21 sessions: sell calls [a promise to sell] struck 2% over that close against all of it; any rise past the strike is paid away in cash, shares kept. Premiums are modelled, not measured. This is where the model is most generous to the seller - see the caveats and the measured Cboe index.

variants.label: The wheel: promise to buy 2% lower until you own SPY, then promise to sell 2% higher until it is taken (premiums modelled, not measured)
variants.note: In cash: sell puts struck 2% under the close; if SPY ends below, you buy at the strike. Holding: sell calls struck 2% over the close; if SPY ends above, the shares go at the strike and you are back in cash. Premiums are modelled, not measured.

model.put_volatility: VIX / 100, nothing added for the skew
model.contracts: puts: account / strike (the full strike sits in bills); calls: one per share held
model.premium_figures: net of the 5% cut; annualised = per-cycle mean x 12 (252 / 21), not compounded. Premium collected is NOT profit: what the options cost at settlement comes out of it (see mean_cycle_result_pct)
model.turnover_counts: option premium traded plus the value of shares that changed hands, each as a share of the account

contract_size_today.note: one option contract covers 100 shares, so one cash-secured put ties up about this much cash (a little less: 100 x the strike)

model_check.note: modelled put-at-the-money variant beside SPY (total return) over the same dates; the page sets these against the published Cboe PUT index

skew_sensitivity.what: put_2pct_below re-run with the put volatility input raised from 1.00 x VIX to 1.15 x VIX (modelled)

vol_input_sensitivity.what: each variant re-run with a different volatility input (a multiple of the VIX); everything else unchanged. Modelled, not measured.
vol_input_sensitivity.why: options at the money usually trade BELOW the VIX and calls above the market lower still, so the published inputs (1.00 x VIX for puts, 0.90 x VIX for calls) make those premiums too rich. Read the rows to see which input brings the model into line with Cboe's measured PUT and BXY indexes.

dividend_sensitivity.what: each variant re-run with SPY's trailing-12-month dividend yield (known at each close) fed into the option model instead of zero

roll_day_sensitivity.what: each variant re-run 21 times, the selling calendar starting 0 to 20 sessions after 2005-01-03 (before its first sale the account just sits in its resting state)

entry_experiment.design: You hold 1.00 of cash and want to own SPY. One start per month (its first session). Idle cash earns Treasury bills; SPY earns its total return (price plus dividends); no trading costs, as in the level-scaling study; put premiums are MODELLED (VIX in, 5% cut), not measured; the end value is counted at the close of the last session of the horizon.

methods_plain.lump: buy everything at the start close
methods_plain.wait_limit_50d: one resting buy order for everything at the 50-day average (each day's limit = the average at the previous close; filled when the day's low reaches it, at the limit or at the open if the open is lower); if the start close is already at or below the average, buy at the start close
methods_plain.put_at_level: every 21 sessions while still in cash, sell a 21-session put on the whole amount struck at the 50-day average (never above 98% nor below 90% of that close); if SPY closes below the strike at expiry you buy at the strike and then just hold; otherwise keep the premium and repeat

columns.mean_pct / median_pct: average and middle result at the end of the horizon, in percent
columns.above_lump_share_pct: share of starts that finished ahead of buying all at once
columns.tied_with_lump_share_pct: share of starts that finished exactly level with it (SPY was already at or under the average on day one, so everything was bought that day)
columns.mean_gap_pts / median_gap_pts: the method's result minus the all-at-once result, in percentage points (minus = it finished behind)
columns.uninvested_end_pct: share of starts where SPY had still not been bought at the end of the horizon
columns.time_invested_pct: average share of the horizon spent holding SPY
columns.mean_premium_collected_pct: modelled premium kept per start, as a percent of the money, summed over the puts sold before SPY was bought
columns.assigned_within_N_pct: share of starts where a put had made you buy SPY within N sessions

entry_experiment.last2_note: 19 monthly starts from October 2024 whose 126-session horizon has already finished (the same starts the level-scaling study uses). The first, 1 Oct 2024, is two sessions before the page's two-year window officially begins on 3 Oct 2024. So few starts, in a market that mostly rose: an illustration, not a statistic.

plain_findings: As MODELLED, selling a put at today's price every month made 10.6% a year since 2005 against 11.0% for simply holding SPY, with a worst fall of -34% against -55%. The modelled premium is too rich (see the caveats): with nine-tenths of the VIX fed in, the same rule makes 7.9% a year.
It softened the crashes; it did not step aside: 2008 -32% (SPY -55%), 2020 -28% (SPY -34%), 2022 -16% (SPY -24%). Its worst single month-long cycle lost 16.3% (2020-02-10 to 2020-03-11, SPY -18.0%).
Last two years, as modelled: +35.5% against +39.6% for SPY and +8.2% for cash.

Premium is not profit: the at-the-money put collected 2.01% of the cash per cycle on average (24% a year), but 32% of cycles ended with SPY under the strike and the average cycle kept 0.88%, bill interest included.

Paid to wait against just waiting (250 monthly starts, valued a year later, premiums modelled): buying at once ended +12.37% on average; one resting order at the 50-day average +11.94%; selling puts at that level +10.64%. The put seller finished ahead of buying at once in 52% of starts, but spent only 56% of the year holding SPY, and in the 22 starts where SPY never came back to the strike it finished 15.8 points behind on average. The premium collected (4.6% of the money) was smaller than the rise it sat out.
One contract is 100 shares: a single cash-secured SPY put ties up about 77,483 dollars today, a QQQ put about 75,620.

caveats: Every premium here is modelled, not measured: we store no option prices. Real quotes differ from the formula, most of all in a panic, when the gap between the buying and selling price of an option widens far beyond the flat 5% assumed here.

The model pays the seller too much where it matters most. The VIX leans heavily on the prices of puts far below the market, so options AT the market usually trade below it, and calls above the market lower still. Fed the VIX as it stands, the at-the-money put and the covered call come out better than the real thing. Where Cboe publishes a measured index for the same strategy (PUT, BXY), believe the index, not this model.

How much of the result is the model: the at-the-money put makes 10.6% a year with the VIX fed in whole, 7.9% at nine-tenths of it and 5.3% at eight-tenths. The covered call makes 13.5% a year as published (SPY itself: 11.0%), 10.9% with the call input at 0.80 x VIX and 8.4% at 0.70. The modelled covered call beating plain SPY is the model talking, not a finding.

For puts well BELOW the market the lean runs the other way: they usually cost more than the VIX implies [the skew]. For a put only 2% below we cannot tell from our own data which side the real price sits on; the re-runs bracket it, from 5.2% a year at 0.90 x VIX to 11.4% at 1.15 x VIX - the input decides the answer.

The model ignores SPY's dividends. That flatters the covered call by about 0.7 points a year and understates the two put rules (0.6 to 0.9 points) and the wheel (0.2 points): the dividend re-run in the extras feeds SPY's dividend yield into the formula and shows each change.

The 21-session calendar starting 3 January 2005 is not the exchange's real expiry calendar (the third Friday), and the result depends on which day the cycle happens to land: the roll-day re-run shows the spread across all 21 possible calendars (1.1 to 2.5 points a year between the luckiest and the unluckiest, depending on the variant).
One SPY contract covers 100 shares, so these rules come in lumps of roughly 77,000 dollars of cash per put at today's price; the test assumes any fraction can be traded.

Real SPY options can be exercised early [American style], chiefly calls just before a dividend; the test treats them as settle-at-expiry only [European style]. Taxes are ignored: option premiums are taxed as short-term gains.

A sold put does not avoid a crash: it takes nearly the full fall beyond the strike, and in return gives up the rise. The stock share shown is the option's equivalent holding [delta] at each close, which climbs toward 100% exactly when SPY is falling. Premium collected is not profit - the settlements come out of it.

In the entry experiment the put strikes sit 2% to 10% below the market, and most of them within 5% of it. That close in we cannot tell from our own data whether the modelled premium is too high or too low; only for the few deeper ones is it likely on the low side.
The entry experiment's last-two-years table has few starts and a half-year horizon, in a market that mostly rose: it shows what happened, not what to expect.
